intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives a way to remember it or warns about a common slip. The section pages gather the ideas, terms and a worked example. Try the example yourself before reading the steps, then answer the recall questions from memory.

sections.title: Why early childhood matters
sections.big_idea: The first 1,000 days are **the fastest window of growth**, and gaps that open there become the base for everything built later.
in_plain_words: Early childhood development covers body, brain and behaviour from conception to about age eight. The first 1,000 days, from conception to a child's second birthday, are the period of fastest brain growth, when good nutrition, health and care pay most and damage is hardest to reverse. Development is cumulative, so an early gap becomes a lower base for later learning.

Brain science, Heckman's economics and the scale of lost potential all support early action. Use each with care. Brain claims are safest at the level of early experience shaping development, and return ratios from old US programmes should not be quoted as if they applied here. Global counts of children at risk rest on stunting and poverty alone, so they are a floor.

diagram.note: the window starts at conception, which programmes most often miss

key_terms.meaning: Growth of the whole child from conception to about age eight.
Conception to the second birthday, the fastest period of brain growth.
Links between brain cells, formed fastest in the earliest years.
Early learning makes later learning easier, so early gains compound.
Economist who showed returns are highest for early investment in disadvantaged children.

worked_example.title: Count the window
worked_example.setup: A child is registered at an anganwadi after birth. How much of the named period has been missed?
steps: Pregnancy is about 270 days, year one 365 and year two 365.
Registration after birth leaves out the pregnancy days.
270 ÷ 1,000 = 0.27, which is more than a quarter of the period.
worked_example.answer: About 27% of the first 1,000 days has passed before registration, so reach pregnant women.

mistakes: Reading the window as a deadline. Children who miss it can and do gain later.
Quoting specific percentages of the brain formed by a given age. They are often overstated.
Quoting return ratios from small US programmes of the 1960s and 70s as if they described a large South Asian system.

recall.q: When does the first 1,000 days window begin?
recall.a: At conception, and it runs to the child's second birthday.

recall.q: What does Heckman's work say about returns?
recall.a: They are highest in early childhood, and remediation later costs more and achieves less.

recall.q: Which risk factors usually build the global estimate of children not reaching their potential?
recall.a: Stunting and extreme poverty, the two risks measured at scale.

recall.q: Why is maternal depression called the neglected risk?
recall.a: It reduces responsive care, is rarely screened in routine services, and a frontline worker could detect it.

sections.title: Domains of development
sections.big_idea: Development has **four fronts** that grow together, so a delay in one spreads to the others.
in_plain_words: The four domains are physical and motor, cognitive, language, and social-emotional. They are labels for observation, and in a real child they are intertwined. A home visit turns each into an ordinary question: can she sit and grasp, does he search for a hidden toy, how many words, does he seek comfort.

Because domains feed each other, a single deficit ripples across all of them. A motor delay reduces exploration, which reduces words and exchanges. Hearing loss appears first as language delay and later as behaviour trouble. Milestones describe wide ranges, and nature and nurture act together, so the environment is the lever programmes can pull.

diagram.caption: four ordinary questions a worker can ask

key_terms.meaning: Knowing an object still exists when hidden.
Managing attention, emotion and impulse: waiting, calming, persisting.
What most children do by a given age; a guide to typical ranges.
Large movements such as sitting, walking and climbing.
Small movements such as the pincer grip and self-feeding.

worked_example.title: Name the domains in one moment
worked_example.setup: A toddler walks across the room, finds a hidden toy, names it and brings it to her mother. Which domains are at work?
steps: Walking across the room: physical and motor.
Finding the hidden toy: cognitive, using object permanence.
Naming it: language.
Bringing it to her mother: social-emotional.
worked_example.answer: All four at once. This is why a single deficit, such as poor nutrition, ripples across every area.

mistakes: Using one missed milestone to label a child as delayed. Look for a pattern, or the loss of a skill.
Treating a language concern as only a language problem. Check hearing.
Reading development as fixed at birth by genes. Genes set a range and the environment decides where in it.

recall.q: Name the four domains of development.
recall.a: Physical and motor, cognitive, language, and social-emotional.

recall.q: What kind of change in a skill should always prompt referral?
recall.a: Regression, the loss of a skill the child previously had.

recall.q: Why is language a useful area to ask about early?
recall.a: Delays are noticeable to caregivers, often signal a broader difficulty, and respond to changes any household can make.

recall.q: What does nature through nurture mean?
recall.a: Genes set possibilities, and nutrition, health, relationships and stimulation decide which are realised.

sections.title: Theories of development
sections.big_idea: Each theory is **a lens**: how children think, learn with others, bond, and live inside their surroundings.
in_plain_words: Piaget saw children as active builders of knowledge who pass through stages, from sensorimotor learning to abstract reasoning. His ages are approximate and his stages contested, and the lasting lesson is that children learn by acting on the world. Vygotsky added that learning is social, and described the zone between what a child does alone and with help.

Scaffolding is the help an adult gives in that zone, and it fades as the child masters the task. Bowlby and Ainsworth explain attachment: a consistent, responsive adult is the secure base from which a child explores. Bronfenbrenner places the child inside nested systems, so a programme working only at the family level leaves four levels untouched.

diagram.caption: four lenses on the same child

key_terms.meaning: The gap between what a child does alone and with help.
Adult support within the zone, withdrawn as the child masters the task.
A trusted caregiver a child can return to for comfort.
Ainsworth's procedure for observing attachment patterns.
The immediate settings: family, anganwadi, peers.

worked_example.title: Match the case to the theory
worked_example.setup: Three observations from a village. Which lens explains each?
steps: A four-year-old uses a stick as a horse and talks to it: Piaget, preoperational stage, which runs from 2 to 7 years.
An older sister gives a hint, then lets her brother finish the puzzle: Vygotsky, scaffolding in the zone.
A mother's worksite has no creche, which limits her time with the baby: Bronfenbrenner, the exosystem.
A baby settles quickly when her grandmother returns: Bowlby, a consistent responsive carer acting as a secure base.
worked_example.answer: Four cases, four lenses. Use more than one lens when you design a programme.

mistakes: Using Strange Situation categories to classify children in the field. The method does not support it.
Reading attachment theory as requiring the biological mother. A consistent responsive carer is what counts.
Supporting the family and ignoring the four wider levels that hold against it.

recall.q: What is the main lesson that survives from Piaget?
recall.a: Children construct understanding by acting on the world.

recall.q: What does the word fades add to the definition of scaffolding?
recall.a: Support is withdrawn as competence grows. Support that never changes produces dependence.

recall.q: Name the four patterns of attachment on the slide.
recall.a: Secure, avoidant, ambivalent or resistant, and disorganised.

recall.q: Which Bronfenbrenner level does a worksite creche act on?
recall.a: The exosystem, through a parent's workplace.

sections.title: Nutrition and the first 1,000 days
sections.big_idea: Nutrition is **developmental infrastructure**, and the two big problems, stunting and wasting, need different programmes.
in_plain_words: Adequate nutrition in pregnancy and the early years supplies the material for brain and body growth. Stunting is low height for age and signals chronic deprivation, best prevented across the first 1,000 days. Wasting is low weight for height and signals acute deprivation that needs treatment now. A child can have both, which carries the highest mortality risk.

Feeding practice decides much of the outcome. Exclusive breastfeeding lasts six months, then complementary feeding adds foods in enough frequency, thickness and variety. Hidden hunger, anaemia and maternal nutrition complete the picture. The loop between generations runs through girls, so adolescent nutrition is also an early-childhood intervention.

key_terms.meaning: Low height for age, a sign of chronic undernutrition.
Low weight for height, a sign of acute undernutrition.
Breast milk only for six months: no water, no other food.
Soft family foods added from six months while nursing continues.
Enough calories but too little iron, vitamin A, iodine, zinc or folate.

worked_example.title: Classify and compare
worked_example.setup: Three children. Illustrative: each feed is one small bowl.
steps: A child with low height for age and normal weight for height is stunted: prevention work over years.
A child who is thin for height after recent illness is wasted: case-finding and treatment this month.
A child who is both stunted and wasted carries the highest mortality risk.
An eight-month child fed at two adult meals: 2 × 1 = 2 bowls a day. Fed four times: 4 × 1 = 4 bowls, double the intake at no extra cost.
worked_example.answer: Different measures need different responses. More frequent feeding is the cheapest fix for complementary feeding.

mistakes: Running a stunting programme and expecting it to treat wasting. They need different programmes.
Counselling a grandmother without understanding her reasons for early water. Counselling that ignores them changes nothing.
Relying on tablets alone for anaemia when the causes are five.

recall.q: What does exclusive breastfeeding mean?
recall.a: Breast milk only, from the first hour, for six months, with no water, honey or ghutti.

recall.q: Which nutrient deficiency in pregnancy causes irreversible impairment?
recall.a: Iodine.

recall.q: Why does fortification outperform behaviour-based approaches at population scale?
recall.a: It asks nothing of the household, even where its per-person effect is smaller.

recall.q: Why are adolescent girls part of the first 1,000 days story?
recall.a: An undernourished girl becomes an undernourished mother and delivers a low-birth-weight daughter, so the cycle must be broken before pregnancy.

sections.title: Health and survival
sections.big_idea: Infection and undernutrition feed each other, so **breaking the loop at any point** helps the whole child.
in_plain_words: A child must survive to develop, and the same investments serve both. Most under-five deaths cluster in the first weeks and months of life from prematurity, birth complications, infection, pneumonia and diarrhoea, all largely preventable. Learn the measures with their denominators: neonatal, infant and under-five mortality are per 1,000 live births, maternal mortality per 100,000.

Immunisation, WASH and a frontline workforce deliver most of the gains. Full immunisation fails at drop-out between first and last dose, which only child-level tracking reveals. Repeated infection and undernutrition form a cycle, so nutrition programmes that ignore infection underperform. Health events carry developmental costs that no health indicator records.

diagram.caption: break the loop with water, feeding, vaccines and treatment

key_terms.meaning: Infant mortality rate: deaths before age one per 1,000 live births.
Under-five mortality rate: deaths before age five per 1,000 live births.
All recommended vaccines received on schedule.
Water, sanitation and hygiene.
The three frontline workers linking families to health and nutrition services.

worked_example.title: Work out a rate
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 3,000 live births in a district in a year, with 90 deaths before age one.
steps: IMR is deaths before age one per 1,000 live births.
90 ÷ 3,000 = 0.03 deaths per birth.
0.03 × 1,000 = 30 per 1,000 live births.
Do not set this beside a maternal figure: 100,000 ÷ 1,000 = 100, a hundred-fold difference in denominators.
worked_example.answer: An IMR of 30 per 1,000 live births. Compare it only with other child rates from the same source.

mistakes: Comparing maternal mortality per 100,000 with child mortality per 1,000 directly.
Quoting an NFHS figure against a different year's SRS figure and calling the gap a trend.
Withholding food from a sick child. Continued feeding and extra meals in recovery break the loop.

recall.q: Which indicator measures deaths in the first 28 days?
recall.a: The neonatal mortality rate, per 1,000 live births.

recall.q: Why do deaths concentrate in the newborn period as other causes fall?
recall.a: Interventions there are more clinical and less amenable to community delivery.

recall.q: What is the fourth WASH element the slide says is often omitted?
recall.a: Safe disposal of child faeces.

recall.q: What kind of tracking tells apart high first-dose and low full immunisation?
recall.a: Tracking individual children instead of sessions held.

sections.title: Early learning and responsive care
sections.big_idea: Children need **talk, play and a responsive adult** as well as food and vaccines, and all three cost almost nothing.
in_plain_words: The brain is built through back-and-forth, so serve and return is the basic unit of learning. The child serves with a look, a babble or a point, and the adult returns promptly. Following the child's lead is what makes it responsiveness. Play and everyday talk fit into time already being spent, and fluent talk in the home language builds language that transfers.

Responsive caregiving is a skill, so it can be taught, but it depends on the caregiver's state. Pre-primary should be play-based and of high quality; enrolment without quality helps little. School readiness is a bundle of health, language and self-regulation, and the school must be ready for the child. Support caregivers with time, mental health care and childcare.

key_terms.meaning: A child's signal and an adult's prompt reply, repeated.
Noticing, understanding and promptly answering a child's signals.
Early childhood care and education, ages three to six.
A bundle of health, language, regulation and social skills.
Pushing formal drill into the preschool years.

worked_example.title: Judge a preschool
worked_example.setup: Four observations from a visit to a pre-primary class.
steps: Children are seated, copying letters: a warning sign.
Activities are play-based and in the home language: a good sign.
Forty children and one untrained worker: a warning sign.
The worker follows each child's lead: a good sign.
2 + 2 = 4 observations: two good, two warning.
worked_example.answer: Two warning signs, drill and ratio, to fix first. Quality decides whether preschool helps, and enrolment alone does not.

mistakes: Counselling the behaviour while ignoring the conditions that block it: exhaustion, depression, hunger and fear.
Using school readiness as a gate to select children into schools.
Addressing only mothers, when fathers, grandmothers and older siblings are present and rarely counselled.

recall.q: What is serve and return?
recall.a: A child's signal, such as a babble or point, followed by an adult's prompt response, repeated many times.

recall.q: Why does the slide say play needs no purchased toys?
recall.a: Utensils, stones, cloth, water and an older sibling supply every kind of play.

recall.q: What does the readiness table reverse?
recall.a: It says the school must be ready for the child, and readiness is no obligation of the child alone.

recall.q: Which structural need do programmes usually answer with messages?
recall.a: Time, the binding constraint for caregivers.

sections.title: The Nurturing Care Framework
sections.big_idea: Five components, **one coherent agenda**, and families who can lead only when systems enable them.
in_plain_words: The Nurturing Care Framework of 2018, from WHO, UNICEF and the World Bank, names five components: good health, adequate nutrition, responsive caregiving, early learning, and security and safety. Its value is coordination, because sectors had each delivered one component and called it ECD. Responsive caregiving sits in the middle because the others are delivered through it.

Bundling services is more effective and cheaper than separate vertical programmes. A single visit can deliver feeding, play and health, and the caregiver hears one message. The limit is the worker's time. Families lead the care, and communities, services and policy must enable them, with maternity leave, childcare and cash transfers acting strongly on the early years.

diagram.caption: families lead, and the layers above must enable them

key_terms.meaning: The five components every young child needs.
Feeding that follows the child's cues; one way responsive care carries nutrition.
The mother and child as one unit of care.
Delivering several components through one worker or visit.
Supportive policies, services, attitudes, income and time for families.

worked_example.title: Find the missing component
worked_example.setup: Four children. Which component is thinnest in each case?
steps: A child is fed and vaccinated but lives in a silent room: responsive caregiving and early learning.
A child is hit at home as discipline: security and safety.
A mother with untreated depression cares for a baby: good health, which covers the caregiver too.
A child's birth was never registered: security and safety, which includes legal identity.
worked_example.answer: Each case shows a component missing even where others are in place. A child needs all five.

mistakes: Reading families lead as moving responsibility onto households. Families can lead only if policy gives them time, income and support.
Adding a fifth task to a visit that already runs short. Something is dropped, usually the new task.
Treating the framework as a new idea. Its value is the shared statement that no single ministry owns the result.

recall.q: Who launched the Nurturing Care Framework and when?
recall.a: WHO, UNICEF and the World Bank, in 2018.

recall.q: Which component is the connective tissue?
recall.a: Responsive caregiving.

recall.q: Why does the framework include the caregiver's health?
recall.a: The dyad is the unit of care, and a depressed or untreated mother is a child-health issue.

recall.q: Name one policy that acts on early childhood without being called ECD.
recall.a: Paid maternity leave, worksite childcare, a functioning PDS or cash transfers.

sections.title: Risk and adversity
sections.big_idea: Risk is not destiny: **one steady adult** buffers adversity, and conditions should change as well as coping.
in_plain_words: Poverty, caregiver depression, home violence, displacement and unsupported disability reach children through food, time, stress and lost services. Risks cluster, so the cost of several together exceeds their sum. Target by risk count and reach households with three or more risks first. Cash transfers act on several rows at once without using a worker's time.

Stress comes in three types. Positive stress is brief with a supportive adult, tolerable stress is serious but buffered, toxic stress is strong, frequent and unbuffered. The buffering relationship decides the outcome. ACEs show a dose-response but cannot label an individual child. Neglect is quiet absence. Resilience grows through at least one stable adult relationship.

diagram.caption: the same event can sit in two boxes depending on the buffer

key_terms.meaning: Prolonged adversity without protective relationships.
Adverse Childhood Experiences, potentially traumatic events in childhood.
Chronic absence of responsive interaction, stimulation or care.
Doing well despite adversity, built through relationships.
A steady adult who makes hardship tolerable.

worked_example.title: Count the risks
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: Household A faces poverty, caregiver depression, home violence and seasonal migration. Household B faces poverty only.
steps: Household A: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 risks.
Household B: 1 risk.
The slide suggests targeting households with three or more risks.
Household A is reached first; household B is a candidate for universal services.
worked_example.answer: Household A has four risks and is reached first. The count helps even without knowing which risk matters most.

mistakes: Using an ACE score to label an individual child. It is a population association.
Importing the original ACE checklist unchanged. It omits caste discrimination, community violence, food insecurity and forced migration.
Saying children are resilient to excuse inaction on conditions adults could change.

recall.q: What decides whether the same hardship is tolerable or toxic?
recall.a: The presence of a buffering adult.

recall.q: Why is neglect often missed?
recall.a: Nothing visible happens: there is no injury, incident or date to record.

recall.q: What is the single strongest protective factor in the research?
recall.a: At least one stable, committed relationship with a supportive adult.

recall.q: How should a worker re-read a child's defiance?
recall.a: As a possible stress response, which changes what an adult does next.

sections.title: India's ECD ecosystem
sections.big_idea: India already has the platform, the anganwadi, so the work is **quality and reach**, especially for the under-threes.
in_plain_words: ICDS, launched in 1975, delivers a package through the anganwadi centre and now sits within Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0. The anganwadi serves children under six, pregnant and lactating women and adolescent girls. Its preschool component most often disappears, because feeding is visible and expected and early learning is neither.

POSHAN Abhiyaan, launched in 2018, added convergence and digital monitoring, with targets that can distort measurement. NEP 2020 makes ECCE a national priority and sets a foundational stage for ages 3 to 8, with the risk of pushing drill downward. The workforce of ASHA, ANM and anganwadi workers carries the system. The largest gap is the under-threes.

diagram.caption: the six services the centre is meant to deliver

key_terms.meaning: Integrated Child Development Services, launched in 1975.
The National Nutrition Mission, launched in 2018.
Early childhood care and education.
Foundational literacy and numeracy.
Departments and workers acting together for one child.

worked_example.title: Find the age gap
worked_example.setup: The first 1,000 days end at about age two. Anganwadi centre attendance begins at three.
steps: The window that matters most closes around age two.
Centre-based attendance starts at three.
3 − 2 = 1 year in which the child is largely unreached.
Home visiting is the standard answer, but it costs worker time.
worked_example.answer: About one year of the most sensitive period falls before the centre reaches the child. Say what the worker will stop doing to make home visits possible.

mistakes: Proposing a parallel structure beside the anganwadi. It is expensive and politically unviable.
Treating measured stunting targets as pure data. Under pressure, measurement gets rounded or skipped.
Assuming convergence works because it is declared. Accountability usually runs by service and never by child.

recall.q: When was ICDS launched?
Which service at the anganwadi most often disappears?
recall.a: Pre-school and stimulation.

recall.q: What does NEP 2020 name as a national priority for ages 3 to 6?
recall.a: Early Childhood Care and Education, within the foundational stage.

recall.q: Why is foundational learning an argument for ECD funding?
recall.a: Foundational learning at Class 3 is largely determined before Class 1.

sections.title: Measuring ECD
sections.big_idea: Decide the **purpose first**, then pick the instrument, since a tool used for the wrong job mislabels children.
in_plain_words: Milestone checks notice one child, a validated screen decides who needs assessment, a specialist diagnoses, and population surveys such as the ECDI describe groups. Mixing these causes most measurement harm. Screening is ethical only where a service exists to refer to, and imported tools can score a lack of crayons as delay.

Population measures tolerate noise and are disaggregated to find who is left behind, while individual measures need precision. The ECDI reports the share of children on track and must never label a child. Always ask which ages, which version, who reported and who is missing. Early identification of disability works only if referral and inclusion are in place.

children.label: Decide on assessment
items: A validated screening tool, such as the ASQ

children.label: Diagnose
items: A specialist, never a screening tool

children.label: Describe a population
items: ECDI or a similar survey module

key_terms.meaning: Tracking milestones to catch large delays early, with no grading.
Ages and Stages Questionnaires, a caregiver-report screening tool.
Early Childhood Development Index used in UNICEF's MICS surveys.
A quick first filter for possible delay.
Break a figure down by wealth, caste, sex or place.

worked_example.title: Match the request to the tool
worked_example.setup: Five requests from a district office.
steps: Notice one child who needs a closer look: a milestone check at a routine contact.
Decide whether a child needs assessment: a validated screening tool.
Confirm a diagnosis: a specialist.
Describe the share of children on track in the state: ECDI or a similar module.
Judge a programme: population measures with a comparison group.
worked_example.answer: Each purpose has its own tool. Write down what the data may not be used for before you collect it.

mistakes: Using a screening tool to diagnose.
Using a population index on an individual child.
Quoting a trend built from two different instrument versions.

recall.q: What does a screening tool do?
recall.a: It flags children who may need fuller assessment. It does not diagnose.

recall.q: What does ECDI report?
recall.a: The share of children developmentally on track, as a population figure.

recall.q: Which question does the slide say decides whether screening is ethical?
recall.a: What happens to a child who screens positive: is there a service?

recall.q: Who is often missing from surveys?
recall.a: Children with disabilities, migrants and the homeless.

sections.title: Practice, equity and reading
sections.big_idea: Good programmes **integrate, start early, support caregivers, build on what exists** and budget the worker's time.
in_plain_words: Five principles guide design: integrate components, start in pregnancy, support caregivers, use the existing platform and measure to learn. The best-evidenced single move is to add responsive-care counselling to an existing nutrition contact. The discipline most proposals skip is to say what will be removed from a worker's day.

Equity means reaching the hardest to reach more, and checking who is missing. Gender runs through feeding, health-seeking and the unpaid care load. Six pitfalls recur, and each shows in a proposal before money is spent. The case for ECD is moral, economic and equity-based, and the deck closes by refusing to ask mothers to compensate for conditions policy could change.

key_terms.meaning: Universal services with extra effort for those excluded.
A recurring design mistake with a visible warning sign.
Reporting results by group to see who is left behind.
Nurturing Care Framework, Lancet series, NFHS, Harvard centre, NEP ECCE.
Equity, economy and rights arguments for the early years.

worked_example.title: Budget the worker's day
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a worker has 8 hours and her current tasks already fill them. A new stimulation task needs 1 hour.
steps: Current load fills the day: 8 hours.
8 + 1 = 9 hours of work in an 8-hour day.
9 − 8 = 1 hour has to come out.
Name the task to remove in the proposal, or the new task will be recorded and not done.
worked_example.answer: One hour must be removed. A proposal that does not say which task goes is adding duties on paper only.

mistakes: Treating nutrition or stimulation as separate programmes. Both are required.
Counting centres built and ignoring quality of care.
Importing an untranslated curriculum or a model without adapting it.

recall.q: Which move does the deck call the best-evidenced single move?
recall.a: Adding responsive-care counselling to an existing nutrition contact.

recall.q: What does progressive universalism mean?
recall.a: Universal services with extra effort for the excluded.

recall.q: What is the first document the reading list recommends?
recall.a: The Nurturing Care Framework.

recall.q: Name two of the five takeaways.
recall.a: Any two of: the window starts at conception; nutrition and stimulation are both required; responsive care is the mechanism; one reliable adult buffers adversity; support caregivers.

notes.2: Eleven sections run from why the early years matter, through domains, theories, nutrition, health and learning, to the Nurturing Care Framework, adversity, India's schemes, measurement and practice. **Section 7 gives the shared framework** and section 9 the Indian delivery system. Read those two first if you work on programmes.
notes.4: ECD covers the whole child from conception to about age eight. The table's two columns are a quick test of any claim you hear. The fourth row explains the urgency: development is **cumulative**, so a gap at two is a lower base for everything after. The second row guards against anxiety about one late milestone.
notes.5: Memorise the window as 270 plus 365 plus 365 days. Programmes most often miss the first term. It begins at conception, so a child registered at an anganwadi has **already missed over a quarter of the period**. Treat the window as the time of greatest sensitivity. It never shuts like a gate.
notes.6: Genes draw the blueprint and experience does the building. Read the left column as a list of things any household can do for almost nothing: respond, feed, keep surroundings predictable and talk. Quote only the safe claim, that **early experience shapes brain development**, and skip specific percentages of the brain formed by a given age.
notes.7: Read the chart for its shape. Synapse formation rises steeply and peaks in the earliest years, so the brain is **most malleable when the child is youngest**. The slide says the numbers are illustrative, so avoid quoting any value from it in a proposal.
notes.8: Heckman's argument is that returns to investment are highest in early childhood and that remediation in adolescence costs more and achieves less. Use the direction freely. Treat the decimal points with care, because the best-known ratios come from small, intensive US programmes and **may not transfer** to your delivery system.
notes.9: Follow the four steps as one chain: skills beget skills, gaps open early, remediation costs more, so invest early. The last row is why the argument travels: **efficiency and equity point the same way**. Keep the caveat in mind. The logic holds for programmes that really deliver responsive interaction and nutrition.
notes.10: The headline says many children miss their potential. That figure is usually built from stunting and poverty alone, so treat it as a floor. The neglected risk in the table is maternal depression. It reduces responsive care and is rarely screened, yet **a frontline worker could realistically detect it**.
notes.12: Treat the four domains as four ordinary questions a worker can ask in a few minutes: can she sit and grasp, does he search for a hidden toy, how many words, does he seek comfort. Language is the **best single area to ask about early**, because delays show and respond to simple changes at home.
notes.13: Remember the direction of motor development: head to toe and centre outward. Gross motor runs from head control through sitting and crawling to walking and running. Fine motor runs from grasping to a pincer grip to scribbling and self-feeding. Use the **sequence** as your guide, since the ages vary normally.
notes.14: Cognition is how children come to understand the world. Look for it in repetition: a child pouring water from cup to cup is running an experiment. Object permanence, knowing a hidden thing still exists, is the example to remember. **Curiosity is the engine**, so protect time and safe things to explore.
notes.15: Learn the four steps in order: cooing and babbling, first words around one year, word explosion with two-word phrases, then sentences and questions. Language grows on a diet of talk, in **any language**. That makes the home language the right place for a family to start.
notes.16: Social-emotional development is attachment, reading feelings, managing emotion, taking turns and building a sense of self. Self-regulation is the part to remember: waiting, calming down, focusing and persisting. The slide calls it the basis of school readiness, so **look for it in how a child waits, calms and persists**.
notes.17: The domains feed one another. A motor delay reduces exploration, which reduces words and exchanges, so it becomes a language delay with no separate cause. The most missed chain is hearing: **a language concern should prompt a hearing check**, since undetected loss shows up years later as a behaviour problem.
notes.18: Milestones are ranges. Use the table's left column: notice, encourage, refer on a pattern, track a population. A delay of a few weeks is rarely alarming. **Regression, the loss of a skill the child already had, always deserves referral.** Never use a chart to rank children against each other.
notes.19: Hold the phrase nature through nurture. Genes set a range and the environment decides where in it a child lands. That is hopeful, because environment can be changed. Watch for **hereditarian talk about caste and community**, which the developmental evidence contradicts.
notes.21: Think of the four theories as four questions about one child: how does she think, learn with others, bond, and live inside her surroundings? No single answer explains a whole child. Treat this slide as the **contents page** for the next seven.
notes.22: Learn the four stages by age: 0 to 2, 2 to 7, 7 to 11, 11 and over. Piaget's ages are approximate and his stages contested, since children manage more, earlier. What survives is that children **build understanding by acting**, so a preschool of handling and sorting suits them.
notes.23: Four rules fall out of Piaget: let children touch and pour, prefer concrete to abstract, treat mistakes as tests of an idea, and match activities to the child's stage as well as age. Use them as a **quick filter** on any activity a programme proposes.
notes.24: Compare the two rows that matter. For Piaget the engine of learning is the child acting on objects. For Vygotsky it is interaction with a more capable person, and language shapes thought. Vygotsky fits mixed-age South Asian homes, and an older sibling teaching a younger one **counts as teaching**.
notes.25: Scaffolding has an operative half: it fades. Do the task with the child, give just enough help, then step back. Support that never changes produces dependence, and adults often keep doing the hard step because it is faster. The zone is narrow, so **judge it afresh each time**.
notes.26: Bowlby's secure base is the adult a child can return to, which gives her the confidence to explore. The left column says one consistent, responsive caregiver is enough. It need not be the biological mother, and in this region it is often a **grandmother, elder sibling or other kin**.
notes.27: Know the four patterns by what the child does on reunion: seeks contact and settles, shows little response, seeks contact but stays unsettled, or behaves in contradictory ways. Use them as ways of thinking only. The method came from one cultural setting, so **a frontline worker should not classify children** by style.
notes.28: Read the system from the child outward. Micro is family, anganwadi and peers, meso the links between them, exo a parent's workplace and services, macro culture and policy, and chrono time. Walk down the levels with any programme and ask **what it does at each**. Most work only at the first.
notes.30: Nutrition is developmental infrastructure. Learn the five nutrients by their failure: protein and energy for length, iron for cognition, iodine for the brain in pregnancy, vitamin A for immunity and vision, zinc for diarrhoea. **Iodine damage is irreversible**, which is why salt iodisation is such a strong public-health buy.
notes.31: Keep the two apart. Stunting is low height for age, chronic, and needs prevention across the first 1,000 days. Wasting is low weight for height, acute, and needs treatment this month. A child can have both, and that carries **the highest mortality risk**, so screen for both.
notes.32: The chart shows direction only, and the slide says its bar values are illustrative. Stunting has fallen across NFHS rounds and stays high, around 29% of under-fives in NFHS-6. Quote that sentence, and **check the source tables** before putting any exact figure on paper.
notes.33: Exclusive means breast milk only for six months: no water, no honey, no ghutti. The table's third row is a labour problem. A woman back at daily-wage work at six weeks cannot breastfeed exclusively however well she is counselled, so **maternity benefit and childcare** are the working intervention.
notes.34: From six months, add foods and keep nursing. The cheapest fix is frequency, since a small stomach cannot take enough at two adult meals. Next is diversity: a spoon of oil and a pulse raise energy and protein with **no new food to buy**. Thin gruel fills a child without nourishing her.
notes.35: Hidden hunger means a child can eat enough calories and still lack iron, vitamin A, iodine or zinc. Match the four approaches to who they reach. Fortification asks nothing of the household, which is why it works at scale, even though **its per-person effect is smaller**.
notes.36: Anaemia has five causes in the table: low iron in the diet, weak tablet adherence, worms and malaria, short birth intervals, and menstrual loss in adolescent girls. A strategy built on tablets alone addresses **one row of five**. Check current NFHS figures before quoting a percentage.
notes.37: The 1,000 days begin in the womb, so the mother is the first nutrition programme. Trace the loop in the closing paragraph: an undernourished girl becomes an undernourished mother and delivers a low-birth-weight daughter. So **adolescent girls are an early-childhood group**, needing nutrition and the means to delay first birth.
notes.39: Children must survive to develop, and the same investments serve both. The right-hand column of the table explains why survival improved: known interventions delivered reliably. The first row, prematurity and birth complications, is now the hardest, so **neonatal mortality falls more slowly** than under-five mortality.
notes.40: Learn the four measures with their denominators: neonatal in the first 28 days, infant before one, under-five before five, all per 1,000 live births, and maternal deaths per 100,000. Comparing a maternal and a child figure directly is **a hundred-fold error**. Name the source whenever you quote a trend.
notes.41: Full immunisation means all recommended vaccines on schedule. The row to remember is drop-out between first and last dose. A district can show high first-dose and low full coverage together, and **only child-level tracking tells them apart**. Access, timing and follow-up cause more missed doses than hesitancy does.
notes.42: The chart shows coverage rising across rounds, with bar values illustrative. Quote the direction and mention the pockets of low coverage. A rising national bar can hide districts that stand still, so **ask for the district tables** before you celebrate.
notes.43: Use WASH as a route: safe water, sanitation, soap and safe disposal of child faeces. The fourth is often missing, so toilet coverage can rise while infant stools still go in the open. On stunting, **be careful**: the trial evidence is mixed and depends on how completely open defecation ends in a community.
notes.44: Trace the loop: poor WASH brings infection, infection lowers appetite and absorption, undernutrition weakens immunity, and weaker immunity invites more infection. You can break it at any point. The practical message is the counter-intuitive one: **keep feeding a sick child**, and add meals in recovery.
notes.45: The three frontline workers are the ASHA, the ANM and the anganwadi worker. Know each one's job from the table, and remember the village health and nutrition day brings them together. Programme quality is largely their time, training and supervision. A new form added with nothing removed **gets recorded and left undone**.
notes.46: Health events carry developmental costs that no health indicator records: repeated diarrhoea, an untreated ear infection, severe malaria and a caregiver's illness. The last row is the one programmes forget. **Treating a depressed caregiver is a child-development intervention.**
notes.48: Survival inputs are commodities that can be procured and counted. Development inputs are behaviour delivered by a person, and rarely measured, so they drop out of results frameworks and then out of programmes. Remember the closing sentence: **a well-fed, fully immunised child in a silent room** is no developmental success.
notes.49: Serve and return is the unit of learning. The child serves with a look, a babble or a point, and the adult returns promptly. Notice the fourth row: **follow the child's lead**, including when she turns away. That separates responsiveness from performing an activity at a child, and a leaflet cannot teach it.
notes.50: Play is learning, and the table maps four kinds of play to what each builds. Pots, stones, cloth and an older sibling supply every row, so no purchased toys are needed. The hard part is persuading time-pressed adults that play is **the learning itself and a break from nothing**.
notes.51: Every practice in the table fits into time already being spent: cooking, bathing, walking. So the ask to a busy household is **talk during existing time**. Say it in the home language, because fluent mother-tongue talk builds capacity that transfers, and halting talk in a second language does the opposite.
notes.52: Responsive caregiving is noticing a signal, reading it correctly and replying promptly and consistently. Aim for responsiveness and accept imperfection: tuning in often enough is enough. It is a skill, so it can be taught. Exhaustion, depression, hunger and fear reduce it, so **counsel the conditions as well as the behaviour**.
notes.53: Read the table as quality signs. Good pre-primary is play-based, in the home language, with a trained adult and small groups. The main risk is downward pressure toward formal drill at age three or four. The evidence is strong for good programmes and close to nil for poor ones, so **raising enrolment alone leaves development unchanged**.
notes.54: Readiness is a bundle: health, curiosity, language, and the ability to settle, follow two steps, focus and manage a small conflict. The last row reverses the usual framing. A first-generation learner in a class of sixty has failed nothing; **the school was unready for her**. Never use readiness as a gate.
notes.55: Responsive care is hard for an exhausted or depressed parent. The table sets structural needs against what programmes offer, which is messages. That mismatch explains programmes with knowledge gains and no behaviour change. **Address fathers, grandmothers and older siblings**, who are present and rarely counselled.
notes.57: The Nurturing Care Framework of 2018 puts health, nutrition, learning, protection and caregiving into one agenda, with caregivers at the centre. Its value is coordination. Cite it in institutional argument, because endorsement by WHO, UNICEF and the World Bank turns a request for stimulation into **the international standard of care**.
notes.58: Memorise the five components: good health, adequate nutrition, responsive caregiving, early learning, and security and safety. A handy test for any proposal is to tick each one. The source is the WHO, UNICEF and World Bank framework of 2018, so **cite it by name**.
notes.59: The chart is schematic and its lesson is balance. A child who is fed and vaccinated but starved of stimulation and care is still not receiving nurturing care. Use the picture to ask of any programme **which component is thinnest**.
notes.60: Component 1 covers the health of the child and the caregiver together. The dyad is the unit of care. The third row is a practical gap: routine contacts weigh and measure children, but few also check milestones, although the visit and the worker are **already there**.
notes.61: Responsive caregiving sits in the middle because the other four are delivered through it: responsive feeding, health-seeking, serve and return, and a predictable adult. Improving it **raises the return on everything else**. It is also the least funded, because it cannot be procured or counted.
notes.62: Component 5 is protection from harm, and the table starts with corporal punishment at home and in centres. Witnessing violence between adults is an adversity in its own right. The last row is cheap and consequential: **birth registration**, since an unregistered child is invisible to every system.
notes.63: Bundling works because the visit is the expensive part, so one contact can deliver feeding, play and health, and the caregiver hears one message. Adding stimulation to a nutrition contact is among the best-evidenced moves. Watch the limit: **a fifth task means something is dropped**, usually the new one.
notes.64: Families lead, and systems enable. Read the last row before you quote the first: families can lead only if policy gives them time, income and support. The strongest ECD policies often carry other names: **paid maternity leave, worksite childcare, the PDS and cash transfers**.
notes.66: Risks arrive in clusters: poverty, caregiver depression, home violence, displacement, unsupported disability. The cost of several together exceeds the sum of the parts. So target by **risk count**: a household with three or more risks is where effort pays most, and you need not know which risk matters most.
notes.67: Poverty reaches children through food, caregivers' time, housing and stress. Rows two and four, the caregiver's hours and mental load, respond better to income support than to counselling. So treat **cash transfers as an early-childhood intervention**, acting on several rows without using a worker's time.
notes.68: Learn the three stress types by the buffer. Positive stress is brief with a supportive adult. Tolerable stress is serious but buffered. Toxic stress is strong, frequent and unbuffered. The same bereavement can be tolerable or toxic, so **the relationship is the intervention**. A child shielded from all challenge builds no regulation.
notes.69: Toxic stress keeps the stress system switched on and affects regulation. The fourth row is the one you can act on today: a primed child reacts fast and recovers slowly, and punishing that deepens it. **Re-read defiance as a stress response.** State the biology carefully, since specific brain claims are contested.
notes.70: ACEs show a dose-response: more adversities, worse later outcomes. Read the right column of the first table as limits. The original list came from a US population and omits caste discrimination, community violence, food insecurity and forced migration. **Never use a score to label a child.**
notes.71: Neglect is absence, so nothing visible happens: no injury, no date, nothing to enter in a record. That is why it goes unrecorded while abuse is counted. Where neglect follows a caregiver's illness, depression or absence at work, **support to that adult is the response**, and wilful neglect needs child protection.
notes.72: Resilience is built through at least one stable, committed adult. The list adds competence, self-regulation and community networks, including faith networks that programmes rarely engage. Do not let it become an excuse. Saying children are resilient has been used to **justify inaction on conditions adults can change**.
notes.73: Five implications close the section: reach the highest-risk households first, support the caregiver, build one reliable relationship, read behaviour as a stress response, and address conditions as well as coping. The last is the discipline of the deck: **refuse the version that asks mothers to cope** with conditions the state could change.
notes.75: ICDS launched in 1975 and works through the anganwadi. It embodied the integrated idea decades before the Nurturing Care Framework. Any proposal must say how it relates to ICDS, because a parallel structure is expensive and politically unviable. It now sits within Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0, so **verify current names**.
notes.76: The anganwadi is the neighbourhood hub, often the only public service in the hamlet. Judge it by the left column and ignore the list of services on the wall. Spend one hour inside: are children playing, is anyone talking to them, does the worker know their names? **Those three observations predict quality.**
notes.77: Six services: supplementary nutrition, pre-school, nutrition and health education, immunisation, health check-ups and referral. Learn who each serves. The slide closes with the warning that pre-school and stimulation are often the weakest links, so **ask which of the six is actually happening**.
notes.78: POSHAN Abhiyaan, from 2018, brought convergence, digital growth monitoring, behaviour change and targets on stunting and anaemia. Each has a watch-out. Digital entry falls to the same worker who runs the preschool, and **targets can distort measurement** through rounding or selective weighing.
notes.79: NEP 2020 names ECCE as a national priority for ages 3 to 6 inside the foundational stage. That strengthens the budget case. The risk is the third row: a foundational-learning push applied to three-year-olds produces the formal drilling that slide 53 warned about, **with policy authority behind it**.
notes.80: Foundational learning at Class 3 is largely settled before Class 1, and the inputs are oral language, play and responsive interaction. The agenda has attention and money, so frame early childhood as **its precondition**. Guard the last row: assessment of foundational skills must stay away from four-year-olds.
notes.81: Convergence fails because accountability runs by service, so no one answers for whether a particular child received all the components. The table lists what convergence requires: shared lists, joint block planning, time in each worker's day, and someone accountable for the child. **Pay, training and workload sit behind all of it.**
notes.82: Start with the fourth row, the largest gap relative to the science. The first 1,000 days end at about age two, but centre attendance starts at three, so the period that matters most is served least. Home visiting is the standard answer. **Say what the worker will stop doing** to make room for it.
notes.84: Match purpose to tool before you pick an instrument: milestone checks to notice, a validated screen to decide on assessment, a specialist to diagnose, ECDI to describe a population, and population measures with a comparison to judge a programme. **Write down what the data may not be used for**, too.
notes.85: Milestone monitoring is surveillance, with no grading. Ask the caregiver, cover all four domains, repeat at each routine contact, refer on a pattern, and explain what to encourage. A visit ending with a caregiver who knows **one specific thing to try** has delivered something. A filled form has delivered data.
notes.86: Screening tools such as the ASQ use caregiver reports to flag children, and they do not diagnose. Run the five checks before adopting one. The last decides ethics: **screening with no service to refer to** produces labelled children and distressed families. Imported items that assume a crayon score missing exposure as delay.
notes.87: Individual and population measures have different purposes. A population module can be brief and imprecise per child because errors cancel across thousands, so it cannot be acted on for one child. National figures are what **put ECD on a budget line**, because SDG 4.2 asks how many children are on track.
notes.88: ECDI is a short caregiver-report module in household surveys, estimating the share of children developmentally on track. Its brevity is a design choice with a cost: it serves populations and must never select or label children. Check the **version**, since items and ages changed in ECDI2030.
notes.89: The chart is illustrative, and the gradient is real: outcomes follow wealth, mother's education, caste and the rural-urban divide. The lesson is one habit, **always disaggregate**. An average can tell you the system works for some children while saying nothing about who is left.
notes.90: Use the five questions on any statistic: which ages, which instrument and version, caregiver report or direct assessment, designed for what level, and who is missing. The last is the recurring gap, since children with severe disabilities, children outside families and mobile households are **least likely to appear** and most at risk.
notes.91: Early identification opens the door to support when gains are greatest. Read the closing line closely: identification with no services is no neutral act. **Build the referral pathway first, then screen.** Expect stigma to hide children, so address it before a screening drive.
notes.93: Five principles, then the table. The last row is the discipline most proposals skip: budget the worker's time and say what will be removed as well as what is added. The second row is the best-evidenced move: **add responsive-care counselling to an existing nutrition contact**.
notes.94: Equity means reaching the hardest to reach more, which the slide calls progressive universalism. Those groups are under-counted as well as under-served, so coverage figures look better than reality. Run one check a year: compare the enrolment list with a village census to **find the children nobody is counting**.
notes.95: Gender enters through the child, in feeding and health-seeking, and through the caregiver. Row three is a cost no child indicator records: an eight-year-old girl caring for a sibling pays for it from her own development. Address fathers and grandmothers explicitly, since **mothers-only messaging reinforces the allocation**.
notes.96: Use the pitfalls table as a proposal review. Each has a visible warning sign: no stimulation component, nothing removed from the worker's day, English materials, letters in a preschool plan, no referral pathway, mothers only. Raise them **in the meeting where the decision is made**, before money is spent.
notes.97: Match the argument to the room: finance wants cheaper later education, education wants foundational learning, health wants a lower later burden, equity mandates want closed gaps. State the rights argument too, because a childhood has worth beyond its use as a future worker. **Source any return ratio** you quote.
notes.98: Start with the Nurturing Care Framework, which is short and free. Then read the Lancet series for the evidence and its limits, the NFHS reports for Indian figures with methods, Harvard's centre for serve and return, and the NEP sections on ECCE. Each row says **what to read it for**.
notes.99: Five takeaways with their sections. Say them aloud without looking: the window starts at conception, nutrition and stimulation together, responsive care is free to deliver, one reliable adult buffers adversity, support caregivers. The discipline underneath is to **never ask mothers to compensate** for conditions that policy could change.
